Retrospective Economic Evaluation of Group
Testing in the COVID-19 Pandemic
Michael Balzer1*, Kainat Khowaja1and Christiane Fuchs1
1Bielefeld University, Faculty of Business Administration and
Economics, Data Science Group, Universit¨ atsstraße 25, Bielefeld, 33615,
NW, Germany.
*Corresponding author(s). E-mail(s): michael.balzer@uni-bielefeld.de;
Abstract
Surveillance of diseases in a pandemic is an important part of public health pol-
icy. Diagnostic testing at the individual level is often infeasible due to resource
constraints. To circumvent these constraints, group testing can be applied. The
economic cost evaluation from the payer’s perspective typically focuses only on
deterministic costs which overlooks the substantial economic impact of produc-
tivity losses resulting from quarantine and workplace disruptions. The objective
of this article is to develop a mathematical model for a retrospective eco-
nomic evaluation of group testing that incorporates both deterministic costs and
income-based economic loss. Group testing algorithms are revisited and simu-
lated at optimized pool sizes to determine the required number of tests. Income
data from the German Socio-Economic Panel are integrated into a mathematical
model to capture the economic loss. Afterward, hybrid Monte Carlo experiments
are conducted by evaluating the economic cost in the Coronavirus disease 2019
pandemic in Germany. Monte Carlo experiments show that the optimal choice
of group testing algorithms changes substantially when income-based economic
losses are included. Evaluations considering only deterministic costs systemati-
cally underestimate the total economic cost. Algorithms with a longer quarantine
duration are less attractive than shorter quarantine duration if income-based
economic loss is accounted for. The findings show that current evaluations under-
estimate the true economic cost. Group testing algorithms with shorter duration
and fewer stages are preferred, even when they require a larger number of tests.
These results underscore the importance of incorporating income-based economic
loss into a mathematical model.
Keywords:Monte Carlo experiments, COVID-19, Pandemics, Economic cost,
Mathematic modeling

1 Introduction
A wide range of pathogens cause infectious diseases which have a profound impact
on human life. The human immunodeficiency virus, chlamydia, gonorrhea or more
recently the late severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) are
examples of such infectious diseases (Pilcher et al, 2005; Datta et al, 2007; Mutesa
et al, 2021). Unsurprisingly, an important part of public health policy consists of the
surveillance of diseases where the goal is to monitor and prevent the rapid spread in
populations (Kline et al, 1989).
Monitoring leverages diagnostic testing where the most common approach relies on
testing individuals in a population by specifically designed protocols. For instance, in
pandemics, testing focuses mainly on ill individuals, whereas asymptomatic or healthy
individuals are neglected. However, if the population to be screened is large, the indi-
vidual testing procedure is often difficult or even impossible to perform given limited
resources (Millioni and Mortarino, 2021). Alternatively, individuals of a population
can be grouped and evaluated on joint test results. If a test indicates that there is no
infected individual in a group, then every individual in that group is directly declared
as negative and thus non-infected. Consequently, should a group include at least one
infected individual, then this group is labeled as positive and further testing is neces-
sary. This algorithmic outline is generally called group testing (GT) (Dorfman, 1943;
Hwang, 1972; Aldridge and Ellis, 2022).
Since the advent of the COVID-19 pandemic, GT has garnered increased attention
due to the decrease in test numbers compared to individual testing. Additionally, GT
algorithms have been associated with a reduction in economic cost and the mitigation
of resource constraint (Eberhardt et al, 2020; Mutesa et al, 2021; Aldridge and Ellis,
2022). For instance, several studies examining SARS-CoV-2 testing in Germany con-
clude that the economic cost savings can be traced back to a reduction in material
costs which are composed of start-up, pre-screening questionnaire and apps as well
as implementation costs (see, for example, Nguyen et al (2021); Simas et al (2021);
Nguyen et al (2023); Pighi et al (2023)).
On the negative side, GT algorithms are accompanied by waiting times for testing
rounds where individuals from positive pools have to be quarantined until declared
negative. However, the economic loss associated with the quarantine duration is
unknown. Although Brandt et al (2024) account for the economic loss associated with
the quarantine duration in a retrospective healthcare study based on sick benefits,
a general economic evaluation of the GT algorithms from the payer’s perspective is
missing.
The aim of this article is to propose a mathematical model for an economic eval-
uation of GT algorithms from the payer’s perspective in Germany which includes
regional, economic and temporal disparities. Furthermore, hybrid Monte Carlo exper-
iments are conducted which combine artificial generation of optimal test numbers for
GT algorithms with a real-world income data set for the economic loss. Particularly,
the mathematical model relies on interpreting the monetary compensation of individ-
uals in the form of their income as the economic loss for the quarantine duration.
Since the incomes in Germany are subject to variation due to spatio-temporal dis-
parities, often unavailable, outdated or subject to measurement error, the data set
2

provided by the Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP) research infrastructure is utilized. The
data set consists of a large-scale panel data study on households and individuals via
questionnaires (German Institute for Economic Research (DIW Berlin), 2022).
Motivated by conjectures in GT literature which suggest that GT algorithms with
longer quarantine duration are generally unlikely to be applied in pandemics, the
hybrid Monte Carlo experiments show that focusing on purely deterministic costs leads
to an underestimation of economic costs (Aldridge and Ellis, 2022). Thus, by tackling
GT algorithms under the assumption that they are embedded in real-world application
settings where resource-constraints and uncertainty are naturally occurring, the results
confirm that GT algorithms with shorter quarantine duration are preferred.
In Section 2, the mathematical model is introduced. Afterwards, Monte Carlo
experiments are conducted in Section 3. Finally, results are concluded and discussed
in Section 4.
2 Methods
2.1 Group Testing algorithms
In Section 1, GT is described as any algorithm that divides a population into disjoint
pools and evaluates results based on joint tests. A variety of GT algorithms have
been developed which follow this algorithmic outline. The focus in this article lies
on well established GT algorithms which garnered profound interest in pandemics.
Particularly, multi-stage Dorfman-type algorithms discussed in (Dorfman, 1943) and
(Patel, 1962) are considered. The practical application in the COVID-19 pandemic of
these GT algorithms has been reviewed in Eberhardt et al (2020); Mutesa et al (2021)
and Aldridge and Ellis (2022).
Generally, GT algorithms can be divided into two types, which are adaptive and
non-adaptive algorithms. Moreover, GT algorithms can be divided further into two
different branches, which are probabilistic and combinatorial GT algorithms. Non-
adaptive GT algorithms are based on designing the testing procedure beforehand such
that intermediate results do not matter in subsequent stages. Combinatorial GT is
more general and assumes a deterministic model but is also often not applicable in
pandemics due to the inherent complex procedure and long-running time of the algo-
rithms. Adaptive GT algorithms rely on stage-wise procedures, where further tests
can only be carried out when the results from the previous testing stages are recov-
ered. Probabilistic GT relies on the assumption that there is a probability distribution
on the number of infected individuals (Sobel and Groll, 1959; Hwang, 1972; Du and
Hwang, 2000; Aldridge et al, 2019; Mutesa et al, 2021). Multi-stage Dorfman-type
algorithms can be described as adaptive, probabilistic GT algorithms, where in the
final stage individual retesting has to be performed to confirm the status of infec-
tion. Such GT algorithms are called trivial or conservative and can more easily be
investigated mathematically (Aldridge and Ellis, 2022).
Generally, computing the number of tests is non-trivial due to the inherent
probabilistic nature in multi-stage Dorfman-type algorithms. However, under certain
assumptions, the expected number of tests can be derived which is useful to find opti-
mal pool sizes. In terms of notation, letp∈(0,1) be the prevalence,q= 1−pthe

Since the considered GT algorithms have multiple stages and test results are not
available instantaneously, individuals have to be quarantined because the status of
their infection remains unclear. From the payer’s perspective, individuals may be
hindered in pursuing their work given their occupation. Therefore, quantifying the
economic loss associated with the quarantine duration becomes a central obstacle. In
the model mathematical model, the economic loss is defined as the compensation an
individual receives despite being unable to work. This definition is motivated by two
perspectives. First, since individuals are unable to work, the companies are effectively
losing productivity for the duration of the quarantine. This leads to effective adverse
effects on the overall production and profit over time. Second, in the COVID-19 pan-
demic in Germany, the German Infection Protection Act stated that individuals had
to be compensated directly from the employer for the quarantine duration. In turn, the
employer could claim the paid compensation from the authority (Bundesministerium
f¨ ur Justiz, 2021).
Two recent healthcare studies utilize a similar definition of economic loss. The
assumption of economic loss based on sick pay has been taken into account in an
estimation of average COVID-19-associated costs per capita based on empirical health
insurance claims for Germany (Brandt et al, 2024). Another study specializing on the
cost evaluation of testing procedures in the COVID-19 pandemic in emergency rooms
in German hospitals takes a similar notion of economic loss into account (Diel and
Nienhaus, 2022).
To mathematically formalize the economic loss and embed it into the mathematical
model, the structural hierarchy and spatial variations of incomes have to be consid-
ered. For instance, the shape of the income distribution in schools will severely differ
from the distribution in large companies. Furthermore, industries are not uniformly

detailed information about the incomes. Additionally, the duration of a stage in a GT
algorithm has to be quantified. For simplicity, the duration is set to exactly one day
in the mathematical model. By construction, every individual in a population has to
be tested in the first stage such that all individuals stay in quarantine for one day.

3 Results
3.1 Empirical setting and data collection
To investigate the effects of changes in parameters in the proposed mathematical
model, hybrid Monte Carlo experiments are conducted which combine variables based
on real-world data such prevalence and income levels and costs that are predetermined.
The empirical setting is concerned with the retrospective economic evaluation of GT in
the COVID-19 pandemic in Germany. Three districts, namely Hamburg, Bremen and
Berlin-Mitte are chosen to exemplify and demonstrate the effects of variable changes in
the mathematical model. The choice of districts is motivated by the available data on
prevalence levels as well as incomes. Particularly, information about prevalence levels
in the German districts are of primary interest which correspond to the geographical
locations in the mathematical model. Thus, a large-scale data set containing seven-
day incidence rates for COVID-19 on district level from the Robert Koch Institute is
utilized (Koch-Institut, 2024).
Since prevalence levels are not readily available in the data set, an approximation
of the point prevalence has to be computed. The point prevalence can be approximated
as the product of the incidence rate and the duration of the infectious disease (Bruce
et al, 2018). Assuming constant arrival of new cases over a period of seven days
combined with a suitable average duration of SARS-CoV-2, the prevalence levels in
German districts can be approximated. However, there is no consensus on the average
duration of SARS-CoV-2. Cevik et al (2021) provide a systematic review and meta-
analysis for the duration of viral shedding in SARS-CoV-2 and find average results
ranging from 14 to 126 days. In a different study, Walsh et al (2020) report that
COVID-19 patients with mild-to-moderate illness are usually infectious until day ten
with some individuals having a longer time frame of infectiousness. Similarly, Rhee
et al (2021) observed that patients with mild to moderate illness remain infectious for
up to 10 days. For those who are severely to critically ill, the infectious period extends
7

to 15 days, with a maximum duration of 20 days. These results are also supported
by the World Health Organization (World Health Organization, 2024). Therefore, 14
days is taken as a reference value in the Monte Carlo experiments. The approximated
point prevalence for the districts of interest can be seen in Figure 2.
The income data set of the SOEP-Core in the most recent version from the year
2021 is additionally utilized. This data set is based on repetitive and representative
surveys with questionnaires on households and individuals from the years 1984 to
2021 in Germany. The central variables of interest are the state of residence, the
monthly gross labor income and the worked hours in a week of an individual in the
years 2019 to 2021 which partially correspond to the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic in
Germany. Since exact information about the daily incomes is not readily available in
the data set, estimation is necessary. Utilizing the worked hours in a week under the
assumption of a typical five day work week on average yields the actual worked daily
hours. Analogous, weekly incomes can be obtained by dividing the monthly gross labor
income by the average work weeks in a year of 4.345. By dividing the weekly incomes
by the actual daily worked hours, daily incomes are obtained. Thus, the final data set
contains 23727 observations and four variables. The computed daily incomes for the
districts of interest can be seen in Figure 3.
Fig. 2Progress of approximated point prevalence values in the COVID-19 pandemic in German districts
Berlin-Mitte, Bremen and Hamburg across the years 2020 to 2024.

3.3 Impact of incomes in German districts
In Figure 4, the effects of different income levels on the ECI in German districts are
presented. The results for Berlin indicate that the ECI ranges from 75 to 155 over
different prevalence values. The three-stage algorithm has the lowest average ECI until
prevalence values of 0.005. However, due to the randomness when drawing incomes
from the empirical distribution, the choice shifts occasionally towards the two-stage
algorithm. For prevalence values larger than 0.005, the preferred choice gradually shifts
towards the two-stage algorithm.
In contrast, the results for Bremen show that the ECI is generally lower, ranging
from values 60 to 120. The lowest average ECI can thus be observed in the three-stage
algorithm until prevalence values of 0.03. Afterwards, the preferred choice gradually
favors the two-stage algorithm. However, the results for Hamburg are closely aligned
to the results of Berlin. The largest deviation can be seen in the range where Berlin
exhibits larger uncertainty than Hamburg. Similar results for Berlin and Hamburg are
unsurprising since the distributions of the incomes in Figure 3 show that the mean

incomes in both districts are similar. However, the deviation in the range can be
attributed to fact that the standard deviation of incomes in Berlin is higher which
leads to an increase in the range for Berlin.
In general, the results indicate that higher incomes shift the preference in terms
of GT algorithms towards fewer numbers of stages. Thus, lower incomes indicate that
the adverse effect of the additional quarantine duration in economic cost is weaker.
Combined with lower number of tests, the results show the preference towards three-
stage algorithms. Similarly, the range is much narrower due to the lower incomes.
Thus, depending on the incomes in a district, payers should utilize two- and three-
stage algorithms for lowering their economic cost. If incomes are high, the two-stage
algorithm is preferred in order to clear individuals faster. Payers with lower incomes
can perform GT for more numbers of stages but should not choose a GT algorithm
with more than three stages.
3.4 Impact of population size
In Figure 5, the results for the impact of varying population sizes can be seen. Given
the similarity of the prevalence values in the considered districts, the focus lies on
Hamburg for brevity in the presentation of the results.
For a population size ofn= 150, the ECI ranges from 140 to 220 throughout
the prevalence values. Almost always, the two-stage algorithm is the optimal choice.
Notable is the erratic behavior occurring in the average ECI. The erratic behavior can
be explained by the underlying permutations in GT algorithms if population sizes are
small. For instance, depending on the optimal pool size, an additional infected indi-
vidual found in a separate, otherwise negative pool leads to a doubling in the number
of tests if all the other infected individuals are condensed in one pool. Consequently, a

3.5 Changes in deterministic costs
In the following, changes in deterministic costs on the ECI are considered. In principle,
changes in the deterministic costs act as a scaling factor in the number of tests.
The mathematical model suggests that the optimal choice tends to GT algorithm
with lower number of tests as the deterministic costs increase. These expectations
are confirmed in Figure 6. Forc v= 150, the ECI ranges from 80 to 180. The two-
stage algorithm is almost always preferred which is as expected since it has the lowest
quarantine duration and thus the lowest economic loss. Note that individual testing

3.6 Changes in outsource costs
Similar to the deterministic costs, changes in outsource costs are investigated in the
following. The mathematical model suggests that the testing capacity is similar to the
deterministic costs, scaling with the difference between the number of tests and the
testing capacity. In principle, GT algorithms with a lower number of tests are preferred
as testing capacity decreases. In Figure 7 the expectations can be confirmed.

Ifτ0= 0, that is, there is no internal testing capacity, then every test has to be

is the preferred GT algorithm. Generally, the range is also quite pronounced. Changes

The results indicate that the number of outsourced tests is low or almost non-existent
for multi-stage GT algorithms. However, the two-stage algorithm becomes occasionally

τ0>250, the ECI ranges from 80 to 150. The optimal choice is almost always the
two-stage algorithm. Outsourcing for multi-stage GT algorithms is never conducted
since the testing capacity is enough to satisfy the demand for tests. Thus, the two-
stage algorithm is preferred due to the higher number of tests and lower quarantine
duration.
3.7 Effects of Changes in Remote Work
From the mathematical model, it can be inferred that changes in remote work have
an effect on the economic loss. In particular,hcan be seen as a scaling factor leading
to an increase in the ECI. The expectation can be seen in Figure 8. Forh= 0, that is,
there is no possibility of remote work, the ECI ranges from 140 to 250. The optimal
choice is always the two-stage algorithm. Thus, the GT algorithm with the lowest
quarantine duration is preferred, albeit permitting disadvantages due to larger number
of tests. Differences in terms of optimal choice can be seen forh= 0.5 where in low to
moderate prevalence situations the three-stage algorithm becomes the preferred choice.
The strong decrease in economic cost based on the economic loss is the main driver
of this change. The number of tests is lower in the three-stage algorithm which paired
with the strong decrease in economic loss leads to a change in the optimal choice. For

for changing values of the remote workh∈ {0,0.5,0.9,1}. Solid lines represents the average ECI.

as before.
The most interesting changes can be seen forh= 1. This corresponds to scenarios
where every individual in a screened population can work remotely. Consequently, the
economic loss is zero. Therefore, this corresponds purely to the evaluation of the deter-
ministic costs. It can be concluded that in low to moderate prevalence situation, the
five-stage algorithm is preferred. In moderate to moderately high prevalence situations,
the four-stage algorithm is the optimal choice. In the very high prevalence situations,
the three-stage algorithm is the optimal choice. Additionally, lowest ECI values are
reached ranging from 10 to 60. Furthermore, the range has decreased substantially.
Unsurprisingly, the best practice from the payer’s perspective is to incorporate a high
percentage of remote work, if possible. This leads to a longer quarantine duration but
since economic loss is non-existent, the lowest ECI due to the lowest number of tests
can be ensured. GT algorithms with many stages are the preferred option. If high
percentages cannot be ensured, the combinations of two-stage and three-stage algo-
rithms should be the preferred choice because these provide a decent trade-off between
number of tests and economic loss.
4 Discussion
The key findings and main contributions of this study are: (a) Deterministic costs are
combined with economic loss for economic evaluation of GT algorithms in pandemics.
To this end, a mathematical model of economic cost is introduced. By proposing a gen-
eral framework for economic loss based on incomes, the inclusion of additional costs
that have been reported in empirical studies by Diel and Nienhaus (2022) and Brandt
et al (2024) are accounted for. (b) The income-based economic loss is motivated from
15

two perspective. Quarantined individuals are unable to work. This results in productiv-
ity losses from the payer’s perspective. Moreover, the compensation can be regulated
by law as in the case of Germany with the Infection Protection Act. Thus, economic
loss is represented by an increase in the health care spending. (c) In the case study
of economic cost in the COVID-19 pandemic in Germany, spatio-temporal variations
are accounted for by utilizing a large-scale income data set on state of residence and
district level. Additionally, COVID-19 data from the Robert Koch Institute is utilized
(German Institute for Economic Research (DIW Berlin), 2022; Koch-Institut, 2024).
(d) Hybrid Monte Carlo experiments confirm that focusing solely on deterministic
costs in the evaluation of the ECI for different GT algorithms leads to severe under-
estimation of underlying, not directly observable costs. The results for the baseline
model in the Monte Carlo experiments show that the optimal choice of GT algorithms
with the lowest ECI consists of a combination of the two- and three-stage algorithm
depending on the prevalence levels and districts. Changes in different parameters lead
to a change in the optimal choice of GT algorithms. Particularly, for very large popu-
lations, the three-stage algorithm whereas for much smaller population the two-stage
algorithm is the optimal choice. Changes in deterministic costs change the optimal
choice from the two- to the three-stage algorithm. For extreme values of determinis-
tic costs, the optimal choice changes further to the four- and the five-stage algorithm.
Furthermore, these changes are accompanied by an increase in the ECI. Changes in
the testing capacity have the exact reverse effect. With an increasing testing capacity,
the favored GT algorithm shifts from three- to two-stage. Moreover, this change is
accompanied with a decrease in the ECI. The most interesting case can be observed
when the remote work parameterhis varied. In this case, the results indicate that
high values of remote work lead to a shift in favor of algorithms with a higher number
of stages. As the percentage of remote work decreases, the decision changes to GT
algorithms with three or two stages. Individual testing is the optimal choice only if the
prevalence values are high or very high. Since the overall prevalence in the scenarios
are always low, individual testing as the optimal choice has not been observed.
In the course of the study, several limitations have become apparent. First, strong
assumptions in Section 2 that need to hold in order to derive the expressions for the
expected number of tests are imposed. Particularly, the assumptions of perfect test-
ing conditions is not realistic but quite convenient for the derivation of the expected
number of tests in GT algorithms. A natural extension is to relax some assumptions
and investigate how the results change. Second, the GT literature recently received
an explosion in work with the development of novel GT algorithms. It is clear that a
departure from established GT algorithms considered in this article is another direc-
tion for future research. Particularly, the so called grid and hypercube algorithms are
promising candidates (Mutesa et al, 2021; Aldridge and Ellis, 2022). Third, the per-
spective of economic loss and thus an increased burden for the health care sector relies
on regulated compensation by law. For countries that do not introduce a law that
ensures the compensation of individuals due to quarantine, only the productivity loss
can be taken into account. The focus on Germany is primarily motivated by the com-
pensation of individuals in quarantine which is written in law (Bundesministerium f¨ ur
Justiz, 2021). Results for different countries are also of interest. On the same note,
16

the case study exemplifies mainly the districts of Berlin, Bremen and Hamburg. Dif-
ferent results are obtained if the district and thus prevalence as well as income levels
change. Fourth, a simplified form of epidemic dynamics is considered while deliberately
ignoring any possible interventions as, for example, vaccines, recovered individuals or
asymptomatic infected individuals. Furthermore, a simple, linear mathematical model
is constructed. However, non-linear relationships in the model might describe real-
world outcomes better. Fifth, only a one-way effect of epidemics has been considered
on the ECI. It is also possible to evaluate scenarios where epidemics and the econ-
omy interact in non-trivial ways. For instance, if the testing capacity at one day is
not reached, the leftover tests can be utilized in later GT algorithms. As such, the
economic situation has an effect on the epidemic state where companies have to gen-
erate a base revenue to perform GT algorithms. Therefore, these feedback relationship
should be considered in a more sophisticated mathematical model. Sixth, besides eco-
nomic cost, the effect of a prolonged quarantine duration on the mental health can be
explored. For example, the mental state of individuals might have an effect on their
performance in their occupation. These questions are left open for further research.

experiments is freely available at the GitHub repository https://github.com/micbalz/

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses a retrospective economic evaluation of group testing during the COVID-19 pandemic. The main points covered are:

*   **Problem:** Individual diagnostic testing during pandemics is often infeasible due to resource constraints. Group testing is a potential solution.
*   **Limitation of Current Evaluations:** Existing economic evaluations of group testing typically only consider deterministic costs and overlook productivity losses from quarantine and workplace disruptions.
*   **Objective:** To develop a mathematical model that incorporates both deterministic costs and income-based economic loss for a retrospective economic evaluation of group testing.
*   **Methodology:**
    *   Revisiting and simulating group testing algorithms at optimized pool sizes to determine the number of tests required.
    *   Integrating income data from the German Socio-Economic Panel into a mathematical model to capture economic loss.
    *   Conducting hybrid Monte Carlo experiments to evaluate economic costs during the COVID-19 pandemic in Germany.
*   **Key Findings:**
    *   The optimal choice of group testing algorithms significantly changes when income-based economic losses are included.
    *   Evaluations considering only deterministic costs systematically underestimate the total economic cost.
    *   Algorithms with longer quarantine durations are less attractive when income-based economic loss is accounted for.
    *   Current evaluations underestimate the true economic cost.
    *   Group testing algorithms with shorter duration and fewer stages are preferred, even if they require more tests.
*   **Conclusion:** It is crucial to incorporate income-based economic loss into mathematical models for accurate economic evaluations of group testing.

structure.title: Introduction
structure.summary: This partial document introduces the concept of infectious diseases and the importance of public health surveillance. It then explains group testing (GT) as an alternative to individual testing for large populations, highlighting its potential for cost reduction and resource efficiency, especially in the context of pandemics like COVID-19. The document acknowledges a drawback of GT: the waiting time for quarantine, and states its aim to propose a mathematical model for an economic evaluation of GT algorithms from a payer's perspective in Germany, incorporating regional, economic, and temporal disparities. It also mentions the use of hybrid Monte Carlo experiments and real-world income data to assess economic loss due to quarantine. The document outlines the structure of the article, with Section 2 detailing the mathematical model and Section 3 presenting the Monte Carlo experiments. Section 2.1 further elaborates on group testing algorithms, focusing on multi-stage Dorfman-type algorithms and categorizing GT algorithms into adaptive/non-adaptive and probabilistic/combinatorial types.

structure.title: Methods
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses the application of Group Testing (GT) algorithms, particularly in the context of pandemics. It highlights the use of Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP) data and Monte Carlo experiments to analyze the economic costs associated with different GT algorithm parameters, specifically quarantine duration. The document suggests that focusing solely on deterministic costs can lead to an underestimation of economic impacts and that GT algorithms with shorter quarantine durations are generally preferred in real-world, resource-constrained settings.

The document outlines its structure, with Section 2 introducing the mathematical model, Section 3 detailing Monte Carlo experiments, and Section 4 presenting conclusions and discussions. It then delves into the methods, specifically focusing on Group Testing algorithms. The text defines GT as a method of dividing populations into pools for joint testing and mentions the relevance of multi-stage Dorfman-type algorithms, citing previous research and their application in the COVID-19 pandemic.

The document further categorizes GT algorithms into adaptive and non-adaptive types, and probabilistic and combinatorial types. It explains that non-adaptive algorithms pre-determine testing procedures, while adaptive algorithms adjust based on intermediate results. Combinatorial GT is described as more general but often impractical due to complexity and long execution times. Probabilistic GT relies on assumptions about the distribution of infected individuals. Multi-stage Dorfman-type algorithms are identified as adaptive, probabilistic GT algorithms that may require individual retesting in the final stage. The document notes that calculating the exact number of tests for these algorithms is complex due to their probabilistic nature, but expected test numbers can be derived under certain assumptions to optimize pool sizes. It introduces the notation for prevalence ($p$) and its complement ($q$).

nodes.title: Group Testing algorithms
nodes.summary:
This partial document focuses on the economic evaluation of Group Testing (GT) algorithms, particularly in the context of pandemics like COVID-19. It introduces the use of large-scale panel data from the Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP) for analysis.

The main points covered are:

*   **Motivation and Findings:** The research is motivated by conjectures in GT literature suggesting longer quarantine durations are unlikely in pandemics. Hybrid Monte Carlo experiments indicate that focusing solely on deterministic costs leads to an underestimation of economic costs. The results confirm that GT algorithms with shorter quarantine durations are preferred when considering real-world settings with resource constraints and uncertainty.
*   **Structure of the Document:** The document outlines its structure, with Section 2 introducing the mathematical model, Section 3 detailing Monte Carlo experiments, and Section 4 presenting conclusions and discussions.
*   **Group Testing Algorithms:** It defines GT algorithms as those that divide populations into pools for joint testing. It specifically discusses multi-stage Dorfman-type algorithms, categorizing them as adaptive, probabilistic GT algorithms. The document also differentiates between adaptive and non-adaptive, and probabilistic and combinatorial GT algorithms.
*   **Mathematical Model for Economic Cost Evaluation:** A mathematical model is developed to evaluate economic costs from a payer's perspective. This model incorporates:
    *   **Deterministic Costs:** Fixed infrastructure/planning costs and variable costs per test.
    *   **Resource Constraints:** An additional cost component for outsourcing tests when testing capacity is exceeded.
    *   **Economic Loss due to Quarantine:** Quantifying the economic loss associated with individuals being unable to work due to quarantine, considering factors like lost productivity and compensation. This loss is formalized by considering income distributions and the duration of quarantine stages.
    *   **Overall Economic Cost Formula:** A comprehensive formula is presented that combines deterministic costs, outsourced test costs (if applicable), and economic loss due to quarantine, adjusted for individuals who can work remotely.
*   **Empirical Setting and Data Collection:** Hybrid Monte Carlo experiments are conducted using real-world data from Germany (Hamburg, Bremen, Berlin-Mitte) to evaluate GT retrospectively during the COVID-19 pandemic. Data sources include seven-day incidence rates from the Robert Koch Institute. The document also discusses the approximation of point prevalence from incidence rates and the challenges in determining the average duration of infectiousness for SARS-CoV-2.

structure.title: Results
structure.summary: This partial document discusses the economic cost of a "GT algorithm" (likely related to group testing or a similar strategy) in different geographical locations. It outlines a mathematical model for calculating this cost, considering factors like daily incomes of quarantined individuals, the proportion of remote workers, and deterministic/outsource costs. The document then transitions to the "Results" section, detailing an empirical setting for evaluating the model. This involves hybrid Monte Carlo experiments using real-world data from Germany during the COVID-19 pandemic. Specifically, it focuses on three districts (Hamburg, Bremen, and Berlin-Mitte) and explains how prevalence data was collected and approximated from the Robert Koch Institute, acknowledging challenges in determining the exact duration of infectiousness for COVID-19.

nodes.title: Empirical setting and data collection
nodes.summary:
This partial document discusses the economic cost evaluation of Group Testing (GT) algorithms, particularly in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic in Germany.

The main points covered are:

*   **Economic Cost Model:** A mathematical model is presented to calculate the overall economic cost of GT algorithms, considering factors like daily incomes in different geographical locations, the duration of quarantine stages, the proportion of individuals working remotely, deterministic costs (fixed and variable), and outsourcing costs.
*   **Empirical Setting and Data Collection:** The study uses hybrid Monte Carlo experiments to investigate the model's parameters. The empirical setting is the COVID-19 pandemic in Germany, focusing on three districts: Hamburg, Bremen, and Berlin-Mitte. Data on prevalence levels (approximated from incidence rates) and daily incomes (estimated from survey data) are collected and processed.
*   **Study Design:** The simulation involves optimizing pool sizes to minimize the expected number of tests. GT algorithms are then simulated for various prevalence levels and geographical locations. A local point-based sensitivity analysis is conducted, with a baseline model defined by specific parameter values. Performance is evaluated using Economic Cost per Individual (ECI) and its range.
*   **Impact of Incomes:** The analysis shows that higher incomes tend to favor GT algorithms with fewer stages (e.g., two-stage) to clear individuals faster, while lower incomes may favor algorithms with more stages (e.g., three-stage) as the economic impact of longer quarantine is less pronounced.
*   **Impact of Population Size:** Varying population sizes reveal that for smaller populations, two-stage algorithms are often optimal, but with erratic behavior due to permutations. As population size increases, the preference shifts towards three-stage algorithms, and the ECI generally increases, especially when testing capacity is limited, suggesting a preference for algorithms with fewer tests and longer quarantine.
*   **Impact of Deterministic Costs:** Changes in deterministic costs act as a scaling factor. Higher deterministic costs tend to favor GT algorithms with fewer tests, aligning with the expectation that the two-stage algorithm is preferred due to its lower quarantine duration and associated economic loss.

nodes.title: Changes in deterministic costs
nodes.summary:
This partial document discusses the economic cost per individual (ECI) for managing the COVID-19 pandemic in Hamburg, focusing on how different factors influence optimal strategies.

**Key points covered:**

*   **Impact of Population Size (n):**
    *   As population size increases, the economic cost (ECI) generally rises, especially for larger populations (n=5000).
    *   For smaller populations (n=500, 1000), a two-stage algorithm is often optimal.
    *   For larger populations (n=5000), a three-stage algorithm becomes more favorable, leading to smoother ECI curves and a reduction in erratic behavior.
    *   The decrease in ECI range with increasing population size is attributed to the weakening of the marginal income effect.
    *   For large populations with rigid testing capacities, GT algorithms with longer quarantine durations and fewer tests are preferred.

*   **Impact of Deterministic Costs (c_v):**
    *   Increasing deterministic costs generally leads to a preference for GT algorithms with a lower number of tests.
    *   At lower deterministic costs (c_v=150), the two-stage algorithm is often preferred due to its shorter quarantine duration.
    *   As deterministic costs increase (e.g., c_v=2000), the three-stage algorithm, and even algorithms with more stages, become optimal because the reduced number of tests outweighs the increased quarantine duration.
    *   Higher deterministic costs also lead to an increase in the absolute range of ECI.

*   **Impact of Outsource Costs:**
    *   Decreasing testing capacity (related to outsource costs) favors GT algorithms with a lower number of tests. This is presented as analogous to the effect of deterministic costs.

The document uses figures (Fig. 5, Fig. 6, Fig. 7) to visualize these effects, showing average ECI with shaded areas representing uncertainty, for varying population sizes, deterministic costs, and implicitly, outsource costs. The baseline model assumes a testing capacity (τ₀) of 750.

nodes.title: Changes in outsource costs
nodes.summary:
This partial document discusses the impact of various factors on the economic cost per individual (ECI) during the COVID-19 pandemic in Hamburg. It analyzes how changes in variable costs (v), testing capacity (τ₀), and remote work (h) influence the optimal choice of testing and quarantine algorithms.

Key points covered include:

*   **Variable Costs (v):** As variable costs increase, the optimal choice shifts towards GT algorithms with more stages and fewer tests, as the economic loss from longer quarantine durations is outweighed by the reduction in testing costs.
*   **Testing Capacity (τ₀):** When internal testing capacity is low or non-existent, outsourcing is necessary, and the three-stage algorithm is often preferred. As testing capacity increases, the two-stage algorithm becomes more favorable due to sufficient internal capacity and a preference for more tests and shorter quarantine durations.
*   **Remote Work (h):** Changes in remote work affect economic loss. A complete lack of remote work favors the two-stage algorithm due to shorter quarantine durations. However, with partial remote work, the three-stage algorithm can become optimal in certain prevalence situations due to a significant decrease in economic loss.

nodes.title: Effects of Changes in Remote Work
nodes.summary:
This partial document discusses the economic cost per individual (ECI) during the COVID-19 pandemic in Hamburg, analyzing the impact of varying testing capacities and remote work policies on the optimal choice of "GT algorithms."

**Key points covered:**

*   **Impact of Testing Capacity (τ₀):**
    *   Low testing capacity (τ₀=0) leads to higher ECI and reliance on outsourced testing. The three-stage algorithm is often preferred.
    *   Increasing testing capacity (τ₀=250) can shift the optimal algorithm, with the two-stage algorithm becoming more favorable, reducing ECI.
    *   Sufficient testing capacity (τ₀>250) generally leads to the two-stage algorithm being optimal, as it allows for more tests and shorter quarantine durations, minimizing ECI. Outsourcing is eliminated.

*   **Impact of Remote Work (h):**
    *   Remote work acts as a scaling factor for economic loss, increasing ECI when it's not possible (h=0). The two-stage algorithm is consistently preferred in this scenario.
    *   Moderate remote work (h=0.5) can lead to the three-stage algorithm becoming preferred in low to moderate prevalence situations due to a strong decrease in economic loss, even with fewer tests.
    *   High remote work (h=0.9) consistently favors the three-stage algorithm.
    *   Full remote work (h=1) results in zero economic loss, making the evaluation purely based on deterministic costs. Different multi-stage algorithms (five, four, and three-stage) become optimal depending on the prevalence level. This scenario yields the lowest ECI and strongly favors incorporating high percentages of remote work.

*   **Discussion of Key Findings:**
    *   The study combines deterministic costs with economic loss for a comprehensive economic evaluation of GT algorithms during pandemics.
    *   A mathematical model for economic cost is introduced, incorporating income-based economic loss and accounting for additional reported costs.

structure.title: Discussion
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses the economic cost of the COVID-19 pandemic in Hamburg, specifically focusing on the impact of remote work on economic cost per individual (ECI). It analyzes how different levels of remote work (h) influence the optimal choice of group testing (GT) algorithms and the resulting ECI. The document highlights that higher remote work percentages lead to zero economic loss and favor GT algorithms with more stages, while lower remote work percentages necessitate a trade-off between the number of tests and economic loss, favoring two- and three-stage algorithms.

The discussion section elaborates on the study's key contributions:
*   **Economic Cost Model:** A mathematical model combining deterministic costs with income-based economic loss is introduced, accounting for productivity losses and healthcare spending due to compensation laws.
*   **Case Study in Germany:** The model is applied to the COVID-19 pandemic in Germany, utilizing income data and COVID-19 data to account for spatio-temporal variations.
*   **Monte Carlo Experiments:** These experiments confirm that solely focusing on deterministic costs underestimates the true economic cost. The optimal GT algorithm choice varies with prevalence levels, district characteristics, population size, deterministic costs, and testing capacity. Remote work significantly influences the preference for GT algorithms with more stages.
*   **Limitations and Future Research:** The document acknowledges limitations such as assumptions of perfect testing conditions, the need to explore novel GT algorithms (e.g., grid and hypercube), the applicability of the model to countries without mandatory quarantine compensation, the focus on specific German districts, simplified epidemic dynamics, the one-way effect of epidemics on ECI, and the exclusion of factors like mental health.
